title: State
summary: Replace conditionals on a status field with objects that own allowed transitions.

body:
Rule. State represents mode-specific behavior as separate types that implement a shared state interface. The context delegates and may switch its current state pointer after an event. Use it when the same method must behave differently across a lifecycle and the transition table is non-trivial.

Why it matters. Status enums with sprawling conditionals duplicate rules and allow illegal moves. State objects make illegal transitions obvious because the method is simply missing on that type. Interviewers look for transition honesty, not just class count.

Worked example. Order context starts in PendingState. Event pay moves PendingState to PaidState. Event ship is allowed only from PaidState into ShippedState; PendingState.ship returns an error. Event cancel is allowed from Pending and Paid into Canceled; Shipped refuses. Trace an order id 1001: create, pay, ship succeeds; create then ship fails without a silent no-op. Compared with a string status switch, each state class lists only the events it understands. For a media player, PlayingState.pause moves to PausedState; calling pause again can be idempotent.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest. When to use. Use state for order lifecycles, connection protocols, workflow engines, and UI modes with strict transitions. Use it when illegal moves must be hard to express in code.

When to refuse. Refuse state objects for a two-value flag. Refuse encoding every tiny boolean as a state class. Refuse transitions that reach into other states private fields. Refuse state when strategy without lifecycle is the real force.
